#350. Czech arms makers set sights on space defense in bid to sustain Ukraine-driven arms boom

Czech arms makers have thrived on demand linked to the war in Ukraine. To sustain their growth, they need to look beyond ammunition and toward new technologies — and even space.

The Czechoslovak Group (CSG) arms maker announced in mid-October that it has acquired a stake in Canadian space technology manufacturer MDA Space.

This space mission is part of the company's bid to continue riding the boom that has transformed its fortunes in recent years.

When it listed on the Amsterdam Stock Exchange earlier this year, CSG soared to become the most valuable company in Central and Eastern Europe, with a market capitalization of €14.6 billion ($16.4 billion), propelling its owner, Michal Strnad, to the top of the region's rich list.

CSG began life as a 1990s startup, selling military surplus amid the collapse of the Warsaw Pact, the military alliance between the Soviet Union and Europe's socialist Eastern Bloc nations, which was founded in 1955 and disbanded in 1991.

It has since grown to become the second-largest producer of ammunition in Europe after Germany's Rheinmetall and now produces across Europe and in the US.

The main driver of the company's rising fortunes has been Russia's war in Ukraine, which has driven a dramatic boom across the Czech defense industry as a whole.

In 2021, the sector's exports totaled €600 million. In 2025, these exports had expanded to €4.7 billion, powered by orders placed by Kyiv and its European allies.

By the end of that year, European states had procured approximately €11 billion worth of military support for Ukraine from Czech defense firms.

Orders to the value of roughly €4 billion have arrived via the Czech Ammunition Initiative, a program that coordinates the transfer of artillery shells to Ukraine.

Amid the avalanche of orders sparked by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, CSG and Czech peers such as STV, Colt CZ and PBS have been busy expanding production to pump out military vehicles and planes, guns, grenades, shells and bullets.

"The war in Ukraine, particularly in its early stages, was especially well suited to Czech firms," Krzysytof Debiec of the Centre for Eastern Studies (OSW) told DW.

Debiec says that this was largely due to the major role that the former Czechoslovakia played in supplying Warsaw Pact countries.

"Specialization in the production of ammunition — including Soviet calibers — the repair of Soviet-era equipment and the manufacture of relatively unsophisticated systems that could be rapidly introduced and were compatible with the Ukrainian army's existing stocks," have all been key, he explained.

At the same time, European states eyeing the threat from the east and broader geopolitical instability are boosting their own defense budgets.

"The shift in US policies vis-a-vis NATO is forcing European nations to increase their defense spending dramatically, and that's another factor" in the Czech defense industry boom, Jan Jires, a former deputy defense minister and now a senior advisor at the International Institute for Strategic Studies, told DW.

However, since launching on the stock exchange, CSG's share price has performed erratically, illustrating the shifting sands on which Czechia's booming defense industry now stands.

The government in Prague has responded to the sector's surge by transferring the defense industry portfolio from the Ministry of Defense to the Ministry of Industry and Trade to align its growing role in exports with national economic and trade policy.

At the same time, the populist ruling coalition that took power a year ago is made up of parties that have either promised to lower support for Ukraine or — in the case of the far-right Freedom and Direct Democracy party (SPD) — are openly pro-Russian.

As a result, the coalition has halted contributions to the Czech Ammunition Initiative and is dragging its feet on raising defense spending to meet NATO targets.

This only limits an already small domestic market, leaving the industry dependent on exports for about 90% of its revenue — the vast bulk of which is still linked to Ukraine — and lacking a stable base for expansion.

"The Czech industry has outgrown the country's financial means," said Jires. "Unlike German, French or British companies, Czech manufacturers cannot rely on domestic demand to make them globally relevant."

Increased global defense spending looks set to continue, but an end to Russia's war in Ukraine, a change in US foreign policy or a calmer geopolitical environment would hit Czech arms manufacturers hard. For this reason, they must ponder what the future of war, and its funding, might look like.

The conflict in Ukraine offers some indicators, having become increasingly focused on swarms of drones and a technological race between Kyiv and Moscow to improve the performance of the unmanned aircraft.

Major questions must now be asked regarding "the size and role of the military, how it is equipped, what should be purchased and when new weaponry can arrive" Andor Sandor, a defense analyst and former commander of Czechia's Military Intelligence Service, told DW.

For a company like CSG, for which bullets and shells currently account for around 60% of sales, these are vital questions.

"Czech companies — many of which still focus on relatively unsophisticated military production — must invest more in innovative manufacturing," said Debiec, who notes that most are well aware of the challenge. "They have reinvested their extraordinary profits and are already more technologically advanced and diversified in their production than they were in 2022."

CSG's acquisition of MDA Space is part of such efforts.

The company, which already held interests in British and German space technology companies, pointed to the close link between the space and defense industries when it announced the deal.

Noting that global government spending on space defense accelerated to €65.83 billion last year, CSG estimates that the overall space economy will triple in size to €1.6 trillion over the next decade.

Developing capabilities in space is "a natural extension" of its activities, the company stated, noting plans for further development in the segment, including a "dedicated space team."

To power such missions, Czech defense companies must make sure they're in a position to tap into funds for defense and space under the next EU budget, which could rise as high as €130 billion, said Jires.

"If they fail to do so, and all this money is grabbed by German, French and Italian companies," he warned, "Czech manufacturers may miss the opportunity to truly scale-up."

#349. No more Cybertrucks; Musk moves on from the angular metallic flop

Tesla wanted to unseat the Ford F-150, instead it made the Edsel look successful.

Elon’s Edsel is no more. Last night, Tesla CEO Elon Musk revealed on social media that his car company is ending its failed attempt to wrest control of the American pickup truck market. The Cybertruck will cease production in the middle of 2027, liberating that space in Tesla’s cavernous factory for other uses—more Cybercabs, most likely.

Musk first revealed the Cybertruck in late 2019, back when Tesla was still trading at a theoretically understandable price-to-earning ratio. The pickup’s unusual angular shape owed more to low-res video game models than any concessions to practicality. At the time, Musk made fanciful claims that the truck would use a stainless steel monocoque construction, telling his audience that “the body and bed don’t do anything useful” on a normal truck. While some race cars use carbon-fiber monocoques for strength and lightness, making a pickup truck with a stainless steel monocoque chassis would only make sense if someone had an awful lot of stainless steel lying around and needed something to do with it all.

The truck was supposed to go on sale for less than $40,000, and Tesla made its usual stratospheric sales predictions that (had they been accurate) the bare metal EVs would be as ubiquitous as the Model 3 and Y.

But development of the Cybertruck was more troubled than usual for Tesla, which struggled heavily to bring both the Model 3 and Y into mass production. Musk demanded “Lego-like precision” from the workers assembling the trucks, but achieving the 10-micron tolerances required by the Danish toy company was not evidently successful, based on what we saw when we experienced our first Cybertruck in reality.

That was in 2023, when Cybertruck headlines were mostly about recalls and stop sales. By then, the truck used a conventional unibody chassis—conventional for Tesla, not for full-size pickup trucks. Toward the end of that year, Musk told his audience that “we dug our grave” with the truck, perhaps the first public acknowledgment that annual sales of a quarter of a million Cybertrucks probably wasn’t going to happen after all.

Sales never took off, and the Cybertruck’s divisive shape became an all-too-visible reminder of the CEO’s role in reshaping the federal government to his liking. Even selling thousands of Cybertrucks to SpaceX couldn’t save the pickup. Now, with America having vociferously rejected Musk’s vision of governance, those wishing to drive something that reminds everyone around them of that vision will only have a few months more to purchase one.

#346. Tesla to 'wind down' production of flop Cybertruck

Elon Musk's electric pickup for the future will start to be consigned to the past next year. The Cybertruck's bulk and crude shape meant it could only pass regulatory standards in more permissive markets.

Tesla owner Elon Musk said on Friday that the company would scale down production of the Cybertruck at its Austin factory in the coming year.

The South African entrepreneur said Tesla would be scaling back production of his futuristic but often-mocked pickup truck and amping up production of what he hopes will soon become a fleet of fully automated taxis.

"Tesla will be winding down production of the cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production," Musk said on his X social media site.

The announcement follows a bruising week for Musk amid the US midterm elections, where Republicans struggled despite his major donations, with his companies losing billions in value by market capitalization as investors sought to ditch stock.

Musk later responded to a complimentary user online who hailed the Cybertruck as the "best vehicle Tesla has ever made," and calling it an "end of an era" by saying: "True."

For years he had poured much of his enthusiastic marketing zeal into promoting the Cybertruck, saying during the 2023 launch "finally, the future will look like the future."

However the oversized body, straight lines and stainless steel and the post-apocalpytic vibe these created also met with widespread criticism and even mockery.

The electric powertrain was probably a barrier to sales in the US, by far the biggest pickup truck market, where Musk had hoped to take on some of the country's top-selling gas-guzzling vehicles like the Ford F150 or the Chevrolet Silverado and the Dodge Ram.

Meanwhile, the car's striking shape, weight and size made it impossible for Tesla to try to crack Europe, where electric vehicles are gaining a much larger market share.

Unlike in the US, EU safety regulations place considerable emphasis not just on people in cars in accidents, but also on the dangers posed to pedestrians who might be hit by a vehicle. That meant it was not possible for Tesla to register and sell the Cybertruck for road use in Europe.

Beyond this, the vehicle's size would likely have rendered it impractical and unpopular on many European roads, where space tends to be at more of a premium.

Depending how quick the wind-down proves to be, the Cybertruck's production run could prove shorter than its five-year R&D phase.

Given its longstanding issues meeting Musk's very public sales and production predictions, Tesla does not publish sales figures broken down by model.

But according to the automotive data platform Kelley Blue Book, the company sold 20,237 Cybertrucks in the US last year, down from 38,965 in 2024.

At launch in 2023, Musk had predicted unit sales nearer a quarter of a million.

For orientation, Ford sold more than 800,000 F-Series pickups in the US last year, a slight boost on 2024's numbers. These vehicles start at less than half the list price of a Cybertruck in the US.

The IPO for SpaceX this year revealed that Musk's second-largest company was comfortably the biggest buyer of Cybertrucks in 2025. It bought vehicles worth $131 million and did not even enjoy a bulk-buy or friends-rate discount, paying list prices for the fleet.

The Cybercab is a vehicular element in Musk's bid to transform Tesla towards a company focused more on AI and robotics than automobilies.

Rather than just featuring the self-drive or driving assistance programs that Musk has been championing for years, the Cybercab has no steering wheels, pedals or mirrors at all and is designed never to have a human in control.

Musk say the model will be the company's main autonomous model and will supply a global network of Robotaxis.

Starting in the past few months, around 300 such vehicles have been registered and have started operating, on approved roads in the Austin area near Tesla's Gigafactory Texas. They're being added to the existing fleet of autonomous Model Y Teslas being used for the purpose, serving in an area known as a geofence of around 680 square kilometers (264 square miles).

#344. I watched a humanoid robot clean my apartment. It felt like a taste of the future.

The startup Tau Robotics is sending humanoid robots to clean San Francisco homes. They still need lots of human guidance, but they’re learning.

I’m not the sort of person who typically pays for a house cleaner. I’m too frugal, and I kind of enjoy putting on a podcast and going to town on my tub with a Magic Eraser. But when I saw an X post about a new humanoid-robot cleaning service in San Francisco, I immediately signed up for the waitlist. I wanted my apartment to feel like The Jetsons, even if just for an hour.

I was also motivated by journalistic interest. In order to ensure an authentic experience, I didn’t tell Tau Robotics, the startup behind the X post, that I was a journalist—though I did use my real name, so it’s possible someone looked me up. Tau’s long-term goal is to make autonomous cleaning robots a reality, but they’re not quite there yet: For now, the robots are piloted remotely by humans, who watch what’s going on via cameras mounted in the robots’ heads and wrists. As the robots clean, they collect data that Tau will use to train up their more independent descendants. Every counter successfully wiped and T-shirt successfully folded will help the models that power the robots learn to do better on the next go-round.

Because this data is so valuable to Tau, the company charges less for cleaning than one might expect for such a cutting-edge product. At the time I booked, Tau was offering $30 for an hourlong cleaning with a single robot; now the charge is $60 per weekly cleaning with two robots, or $100 for a one-time visit. But even at the cheaper rate of $30 per hour, Tau’s robots aren’t a great bargain. They are thorough but slow, so if you, like me, are tempted to stand around watching them for their entire visit, it would probably be a better use of your time to just take care of the cleaning yourself.

But the robots are physically capable of cleaning, and they’re undeniably cute. Tau has armed each four-and-a-half-foot-tall robot with a 3D-printed “head” with antennae that allow it to communicate with Tau’s headquarters, as well as two 3D-printed claw “hands” (the more humanlike alternatives apparently aren’t durable enough, and claws do surprisingly well for most cleaning tasks). Mine was wearing a Tau Robotics shirt, and grippy socks so that it didn’t scratch hardwood floors.

With all the human support they need, the robots are closer to radio-controlled cars than Waymos. Many tasks, such as making the bed and folding laundry, require what’s called kinematic guidance: The human pilot performs the necessary motions, and sensors transmit those movements to the robot, which copies them. These kinematically guided tasks produce especially valuable training data. Tau’s AI models might not have solved laundry folding yet, but learning from the examples of robots that have completed the task in the real world is how they’ll get there.

But according to Tau cofounder Cornelia Weinzierl, to whom I came clean as a journalist a few weeks after the cleaning, the robot can already complete some other tasks—such as vacuuming and mopping—without any human help. If Tau succeeds in using all the data it is collecting to train truly autonomous cleaning robots, they could even become San Francisco’s newest tech tourist attraction as Waymos become more commonplace countrywide.

The cleaning robot that came to my building last month was already a bit of a spectacle. It arrived in a blue minivan, out of which it was helped by Weinzierl and another Tau employee. That’s when the robot encountered its first obstacle: the eight stairs leading up to the building’s front door. I’d come down to greet Weinzierl and the robot, so I had a front-row seat to its struggles with my steps. It climbed as if it were drunk. Each successful step was as likely as not to be followed by a stumbling backward stagger that erased all its progress—though, impressively, it never entirely lost its footing.

When I later discussed my experience with Weinzierl, she explained that the robot sometimes walks strangely because it is operated remotely from Tau’s headquarters, and the short signal transmission delay can affect its coordination. “The amount of work and time that we spend just optimizing, for example, timings and connectivity is crazy,” she said.

Inside, the carpeted staircase leading up to my apartment defeated the robot entirely, and Weinzierl had to lug it up the last few steps. This, it turned out, was not typical. As the robot cleaned, it repeatedly stalled out, something Weinzierl attributed to it overheating in the unseasonably hot weather—until she heard from one of her colleagues that the heat had shut down not the robot but the equipment that its human controller was using to watch its progress through my apartment. Without remote assistance, the robot couldn’t clean, and so it, and Weinzierl, departed before my booked hour was up. (Back in September, Weinzierl or another Tau representative remained with the robot throughout its visit, but she says that’s no longer necessary.)

In the hour it was there, it did a creditable job of cleaning my kitchen (though it didn’t brave the stove) and even saved me my most dreaded cleaning task, the toilet. That was its most impressive performance: Three times the head fell off its toilet cleaning wand, and three times it managed to reattach it by poking around with the handle until it made contact at just the right angle.

The robot is still rough around the edges, which is to be expected for a product in beta. It repeatedly left my taps dripping, it knocked over a (closed) bottle of olive oil, and it couldn’t manage to right an air purifier that it had toppled. But I easily forgave all those missteps because of how charming it was. As I watched it wipe down my countertops, I felt the same fond gratitude that I feel when a Waymo delivers me safely home after a night out.

Still, it’s not all slapstick and whimsy. If Tau Robotics or its competitors succeeds in training robots to clean autonomously and inexpensively, people could lose their livelihoods, and the United States is a long way away from implementing policies to take care of those left unemployed by AI.

But Weinzierl maintains that someday turning over cleaning work to robots could make a lot of sense. “Cleaning is not a job that a lot of people really actively want to be doing—there’s high turnover, there’s a high risk of injury,” she said when we spoke after the cleanings. “We need people, and we don’t have them, and no one wants to do it.” She said that the company is also starting to consider someday deploying the robots for other dangerous or physically challenging jobs, such as mold remediation and home health care.

Tau Robotics still has a long way to go: The amount of data needed to train robots to do the varied and complicated tasks of apartment cleaning is probably enormous, and the company has completed only a couple hundred cleanings so far. But it’s remarkable that there are now humanoid robots able to clean your toilets and mop your floors, even if they need quite a bit of human help to do so. The Jetsons no longer feels quite so far away.

Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible.

#343. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang summoned by Congress over Chinese espionage concerns

Lawmakers want answers about Jensen Huang’s ties to an alleged Chinese intelligence asset.

Top Republican lawmakers have asked Jensen Huang to appear before Congress to answer questions after it was reported that US intelligence officials believe Nvidia’s chief executive has been targeted by a Chinese spying operation.

The chairs of the House committees on China, foreign affairs, and intelligence wrote to Huang this week asking him to appear before a joint closed-door briefing for their committees on November 18.

“Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the People’s Republic of China’s access to sensitive US technology and information,” representatives John Moolenaar, Brian Mast, and Rick Crawford wrote.

“The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge US technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress. It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which US national security has been placed at risk,” the lawmakers added.

The New York Times last week wrote that US intelligence officials believed Huang had been the target of a Chinese spy operation. The concerns center on a Chinese woman named Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud company that has bought billions of dollars of Nvidia’s chips.

Nvidia has rejected the claims and on Thursday would not say if Huang would appear before Congress. “Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job. Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” the company said.

“Our regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information—not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets—and zero information relevant to national security,” it added.

The lawmakers said they wanted Huang to discuss the security protocols Nvidia had in place to protect against “foreign adversary espionage.” The company said its chief executive had an “outstanding security team” that travels with him.

The New York Times said Huang had not received a “defensive briefing,” which the intelligence community usually, but not always, provides potential espionage targets to warn them about the activity.

Nvidia said it was confident that the US government would have let the company know if it thought a person was a threat to US industry and that it often receives updates from Washington about people of concern.

The US has previously scrutinized Megaspeed, founded in 2023 as a spin-off from a Chinese gaming company, for potential chip smuggling, although no charges followed.

Nvidia launched its own unannounced on-site inspections at Megaspeed in Singapore when it became aware of the US concerns, but the internal probe found no evidence of its chips being diverted into China, said people familiar with the matter.

The company’s supply chain has come under increasing scrutiny as US export controls have prompted increased smuggling of its chips. Earlier this year Wally Liaw, a co-founder of Supermicro, one of Nvidia’s key supply chain partners, was arrested in the US and charged with smuggling Nvidia chips into China. He denies any wrongdoing and has pleaded not guilty.

After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

#342. 8 Best Computer Speakers (2026) After Testing 30 Pairs

Good computer speakers can make for a quick desktop upgrade. Sound is often overlooked when people buy a PC. Some folks prefer headphones, others stick with those old, battered speakers they inherited, and some rely on the awful built-in speaker in their monitor. With any of the speakers in this list, you can enhance voices in video calls and movies, tease out greater depth in your favorite music, and provide spatial awareness in games. After several months of testing, I've narrowed my selection across various budgets and preferences. Whether you want a soundbar for your computer, a pair of speakers, or a surround sound system, you can find it here.

Be sure to check out our many other audio guides, like the Best Soundbars, Best Bluetooth Speakers, Best Wireless Headphones, Best Gaming Headsets, and Best Bookshelf Speakers.

Updated November 2026: I added speakers from Creative, a mention for speakers from Pioneer, and updated prices.

After testing more than 30 computer speakers and soundbars over the last few years, I always return to the Audioengine A2+. With an elegant design and quality construction, they are compact enough for my busy desktop. But don’t be fooled by the small stature—these speakers pack a serious punch. The clarity in the higher registers is excellent, but there’s also depth and accuracy in the mids. While the lack of a subwoofer means the bass can be a little shallow, it’s not distractingly so. Music is where the Audioengine A2+ shines, but I had no trouble hearing cloaked Elites with positional sound in Halo Infinite, and voices came through crisp and clear during in-game chat, video calls, and movies.

Connectivity is well rounded, but just watch out for jumps in volume with different input devices. The volume knob, which also turns the speakers on or off, is a little awkward behind the left speaker, and there’s no remote, but I have no other complaints about these PC speakers. You can also upgrade the A2+ by adding a subwoofer and 15-degree stands. Audioengine updated the A2+ in 2025, making the best even better by adding Bluetooth 5.3, 24-bit audio, and USB-C connectivity. There’s also a built-in USB DAC (digital-to-analog converter), so USB-C is the best way to connect your PC or laptop. Ultimately, these are the best computer speakers for most people because they strike the perfect balance of style, power, features, and price.

With a properly compact form, 6.5 x 4.3 x 4.2 inches (165 x 112 x 109 mm), these cute wee computer speakers can squeeze onto the busiest desktops. There’s an elegance to the molded plastic design with rubbery feet, and the Kanto UKI speakers come in a couple of fun colors (blue or green), alongside the classic black or white. More importantly these speakers produce rich, warm, and detailed sound, with surprisingly good bass. They served me well for music, games, and video calls.

I connected the speakers and plugged the right one into my PC via USB-C (no cable supplied), but there’s also a pair of RCA inputs, a subwoofer output, a 3.5 mm headphone port around front, and support for Bluetooth 5.0. Pairing and streaming from my phone was quick and easy. I appreciated the simple volume knob on the front of the right speaker that you press the switch modes. Desktop stands ($30) are available (sold separately) to angle these speakers at your ears, and they’re probably worth snagging, though there is also a rear screw mount hole.

Boasting a big sound for such a compact set of speakers, the iLoud Micro Monitors come recommended by WIRED's resident audiophiles. These speakers impressed me right from the simple setup (plug in the 3.5-mm audio output). The sound is well-balanced, with plenty of detail in the warm mids and sparkly highs. Even the bass response is good, considering there’s no subwoofer. I love the tiny fold-out feet, enabling you to angle them up for a better sound. There is also Bluetooth support (A2DP) to stream from your phone or other devices. The iLoud Micro Monitors do a great job with music, movies, and games.

But the design might not be for everyone; I don’t like the big iLoud logo on the side. You also have to reach around the back of the left speaker for the power switch, volume dial, and Bluetooth button, though I like the straightforwardness of these controls. There are also three switches to tweak EQ settings, but these speakers are basically plug-and-play. There is no USB port or built-in DAC.

Creative has a long history of affordable but decent-sounding speakers, and the XF1 proves it has not lost its touch. These are terrifically well-rounded PC speakers for the money. Relatively compact, they come with lovely cork speaker stands for a 15-degree angle. The sound is warm, with a decent thump of bass (there’s also an optional subwoofer output port), pleasing detail, and the ability to fill a room without distorting too much when you crank up the volume. Creative’s Nexus app (Windows, Android, macOS, iOS) gives you a 10-band parametric equalizer, so you can dial in the sound you want, or select one of the presets—and there are more than 100. These worked great for my day-to-day, meetings, videos, and some gaming. Playing music was the only time I felt a slight step down from my top pick.

Connectivity is also impressive with USB-C (which will be best for most folks), 3.5 mm line-in, and Bluetooth 6.0, as well as sub out. You hold down the power button on the right speaker to turn them on and off, and press it to cycle through the modes. I found powering down a little annoying, as it switches mode if you don’t hold down long enough. But that's a minor complaint. There’s also an energy-saving mode that powers down after 15 minutes of inactivity, but you can switch it off with a physical switch on the back. These speakers narrowly unseat the Edifier M60 (see below) in this category, largely because they are a bit cheaper for a very similar overall package. The XF1 justify the full $180 retail price, but I have already seen these drop as low as $130, which is a total bargain.

You don’t have to spend big to get a decent set of computer speakers, as Edifier proves with the G2000. Angled to fire sound up at you, these speakers have LED lighting on the back and a compact form that makes them easy to fit on a crowded desk. My test speakers were white, but you can also find them in black, pink, or red. Controls on the right speaker include a switch-like volume rocker and a mode button that cycles between music, movies, and games. Long-press the mode button to cycle LED lighting effects (there are 12). There is distortion on anything bassy, and the G2000 are a bit muddy on the high end. Because the sound imaging is far from precise, it can be tough to pinpoint sounds spatially. This is particularly noticeable with movies and games.

Connectivity options are solid, with USB, 3.5-mm aux, and Bluetooth 4.2. There is also a sub-out for adding a subwoofer, and they really need one if you want a deep rumble. Unfortunately, when you power up these speakers, they play a silly revving race car sound. I also dislike the volume rocker. (Why can't it just be a knob?) The Edifier G2000 can’t compete with our top picks here, but for the money, these compact speakers are impressive, and they offer a nice upgrade over our budget pick below. The RRP on these has crept up to $130, but they are often on sale, so I recommend you don't pay more than $100 for them.

These tiny, cute, affordable computer speakers from Creative have a lovely orb-shaped design with a gold-colored cutout contrasting the black or white exterior. Angled up to fire sound at your ears, and just 4.8 inches tall, these speakers fit on the most crowded desktops. The right speaker has a volume control and a gain switch. WIRED reviewer Nena Farell raved about these speakers and was impressed by their volume and sound quality, considering the price.

Connectivity options include USB-C, 3.5-mm aux, or Bluetooth 5.0. The box includes a USB-C to USB-A adapter, but you need a port that can provide enough power to get the most out of these speakers. Bass is inevitably lacking, and some distortion can kick in at higher volumes. Creative also offers the even cheaper V2 if you don’t need Bluetooth.

The latest compact soundbar from Creative is my favorite from the company so far. This affordable 2.1-channel soundbar and subwoofer system has been hooked up to my desktop computer via USB for the last few weeks, and I’m pleasantly surprised by its performance. The near field mode is ideal for desktop use, and I enjoyed using the Stage Pro for gaming and movies. Voices come through clearly, and there’s a deep rumble of bass, courtesy of the subwoofer. (The subwoofer is large, but tall and thin, so it easily fit beneath my desk). Music sounds good in general, though lacking the warmth, stereo separation, and clarity of our top picks.

Connectivity options include HDMI ARC with CEC, Bluetooth 5.3, optical-in, 3.5-mm aux, and USB audio, so you can also use this soundbar with your TV in a home theater setup or with your smartphone. There are controls on top, and you get a slim remote that thankfully includes the option to turn the display off. The Creative Stage Pro looks smart and fits neatly beneath my superwide monitor. It can be tough to find room for speakers on my desk, as I have a vertical monitor to the left. A soundbar can be a better fit if you have a similar setup using monitor arms. The Creative Stage Pro is a big improvement over previous Creative soundbars I tested (see below), and it’s a bargain if you’re set on a soundbar. Read our Best Soundbars guide for other picks.

As a fan of SteelSeries, makers of some of the best gaming mice, and the Apex Pro keyboard I use, I was excited to try its speaker lineup. The Arena 9 is SteelSeries' top-of-the-line surround sound system. It includes a central speaker flanked by a pair of front speakers with LED zones and a control unit, all of which plug into a large subwoofer. A pair of rear speakers connects to each other and a separate power outlet, but they connect to the rest of the system wirelessly, so you don’t have to run long cables. The Arena 9 speakers are fine for music, but the real reason to get a surround system is for movies or games. They elevated the epic battle scene as House Atreides falls in Dune and helped me react in the nick of time when Banished troops flanked me in Halo Infinite. Only a good set of headphones can provide better spatial sound.

The SteelSeries Arena 9 connects to a computer via a single USB cable, but there’s also an 3.5-mm aux and optical-in and -out ports. There are no controls on the speakers because you get a wired control unit with a touchscreen that acts as a volume dial by default, but can also be used to tweak EQ, lighting, and system settings. You can also dig into this on your computer via the SteelSeries GG software. The Prism RGB lighting can sync with the rest of your SteelSeries gear, with a huge range of animated effects, colors, and even the option to match the colors from your screen. Sadly, there are only four zones of LEDs (two on each front speaker), so it's not like the entire setup lights up. You will also need quite a bit of desk space and suitable spots for those rear speakers, but if you crave surround sound in your games, the Arena 9 is worth the hassle.

There are tons of computer speakers on the market, and many of the ones I tested are perfectly fine, but don't deserve a spot above for one reason or another.

Pioneer DJ DM-40D-BT for $239: Designed as entry-level speakers for bedroom DJs, the Pioneer DJ DM-40D-BTs sport a molded black plastic front with an MDF cabinet, but they feel well-built and solid. There’s a 4-inch fiberglass woofer with a 0.75-inch soft‑dome tweeter, and a class‑D amplifier with DSP (digital signal processing). Input options are RCA, 3.5-mm stereo mini, or Bluetooth 5.0, with a 3.5-mm headphone port in front, a simple volume knob, and a Bluetooth button. On the back of the control speaker, there’s a DJ/Production switch, which dials up the boomy bass. The sound quality is decent for the money, but they’re a bit too big for my desktop. If you need a budget option for music production to pair with a laptop, they might be a good shout, though the IK Multimedia iLoud Micro Monitors above are better if you can find the extra cash.

Edifier M60 for $200: Close to matching my top picks in sound quality, but significantly cheaper, the Edifier M60 speakers produce a rich, clear sound that persists when you crank the volume. The bass is decent, considering the lack of a subwoofer, but it can get muddy and a bit rattly. You have three connection options, including USB-C, 3.5 mm, or Bluetooth 5.3. My test music playlist sounded great on these speakers, and only the rumbly bass distracted me in games and movies, though they come with angled stands that point them at your ears and reduce vibrations. The M60 speakers are also the perfect size for most desktops. On the downside, the touch controls are a little annoying (you have to hold down for three seconds to power on/off or change mode), and the Edifier ConneX app for Android (also available on iOS) was a little flaky, though it offered some handy customization options and a six-band equalizer. Overall, these speakers are a solid option if this is your budget.

Creative Pebble Nova for $266: These eye-catching orb-shaped speakers with RGB rings around the base are a statement piece for your desk. They are big, angled at 45 degrees, and you have the choice of a flat base or elevated stands. They light up, produce a pleasant sound that’s rich across the board and with real depth, and can, frankly, get far too loud for your desktop. I was also impressed by the virtual surround sound for gaming. Don’t make the mistake of thinking the Creative App is superfluous, because it’s packed with options, from an equalizer to dialogue enhancement to RGB lighting controls. While I love the stand, it made them too tall for my desk because of my dual monitors. I also found the touch controls a bit finicky, and I advise switching off the power saving mode.

Ruark MR1 MK3 for $599: Perfect for a retro vibe, the styling includes a fabric front, and black finish with a dial on top. With a fluid and expansive soundstage, music sounds great on these speakers, and even without a subwoofer, there’s a decent rumble of bass. I found Ruark’s speakers equally pleasing for watching movies and video calls, as voice clarity is excellent, though I experienced some slight distortion with deep voices during meetings. They are also quite large, maybe too large for some desks.

OXS Thunder Pro for $600: With a compact design, sci-fi styling that includes RGB lighting, and no separate subwoofer, I was unsure what to expect from this soundbar. The Thunder Pro is 24 inches long and just 3 inches tall, so slotted into place perfectly under my monitor. It comes with a wired control dial, a remote control, and extra feet in the box to angle it. I was immediately impressed when the bass of Dead Prez’s “Hip-Hop” kicked in, bouncing the passive radiators up and down. The sound is expansive, the bass is far better than it has any right to be without a large subwoofer, and the highs are surprisingly crisp. This soundbar is Dolby Atmos-certified and has three distinct gaming modes. The first-person shooter mode offered excellent spatial sound, allowing me to hear the footsteps and grunts of a cloaked Elite in Halo Infinite just in time to avoid being impaled. Connectivity is comprehensive with USB-A and USB-C, 3.5-mm aux, Bluetooth 5.0, two HDMI ports (one eARC), a mic-in port, and a headphone jack. All that’s missing is the option to hook up a subwoofer. The wired control unit lights up, acts as a volume dial and power button, and has EQ and mode buttons on the back. While the OXS Thunder Pro impressed, you will get better sound, especially for music, if you buy separate speakers and a subwoofer.

Razer Nommo V2 Pro for $438: Stick to one brand for all your gaming gear, and it’s easier to achieve harmony. Plus, you only need one app to configure everything. If Razer is your jam, the Nommo V2 Pro is a 2.1 system with tempting bells and whistles. These stylish cylindrical speakers fire light out the back and tilt up towards your ears. The chunky subwoofer is wireless, which could be handy if you prefer to keep the space under your desk free. The wireless control puck acts as a volume dial, and you can press it to mute, play, or skip. You can expect booming bass and rich mids, but there’s a little crispness lacking in the highs, particularly when you crank the volume up. The sound profile is well-suited to action movies and games, with a deep bass rumble that you feel in the pit of your stomach. Connectivity is limited to USB or Bluetooth 5.3. I had some setup issues with the wireless control puck, but after a few attempts, the new firmware was installed successfully. I still found it a bit flaky and didn’t like having to hold it down to turn the speakers on. (They switch off automatically unless you deactivate the power-saving setting.) While Razer Chroma RGB now supports more than 300 games, offers various effects, and an ambient awareness mode that reacts to your screen, there are only two lighting zones (one for each speaker). Unfortunately, the Razer Synapse software is the only way to get at some settings, and it feels bloated and sometimes hogs system resources.

Logitech G560 Lightsync for $250: Folks who prefer Logitech gear should consider the G560 Lightsync. This 2.1 system comprises a huge subwoofer and two speakers with an attractive curved loop design. The speakers project RGB lighting onto the wall behind them. Sound-wise, the bass is dominant and the soundstage lacks definition, but you can play around with the equalizer or use the presets Logitech provides. For movies and gaming, the G560 does better, with DTS:X Ultra virtual surround sound to emulate larger systems. There’s a good thump of bass for explosions, and they provide a decent positional sense in games. These speakers connect via USB, but there’s also a 3.5-mm aux port and support for Bluetooth 4.1. Sadly, for lighting fans, you only get four zones of LEDs here, but there are lots of presets and colors to choose from, and you can have them react to the onscreen action. While these speakers don’t grab me, with the bass bossing the show, they are decent value, particularly as the price has dropped significantly since they were first released.

SteelSeries Arena 7 for $380: The SteelSeries Arena 7 boasts great sound and real versatility. This 2.1 system is the sweet spot in the SteelSeries Arena lineup, as it adds a chunky subwoofer and RGB lighting over the Arena 3, but is still relatively affordable. Simply plug in the USB and attach the pear-shaped speakers to the subwoofer. The adjustable speakers look interesting, with RGB lighting around the base and back, and a mode button and volume dial on the right speaker (headphone port behind it). This system produces a soundstage with clarity and precision, but can sound too bassy and flat, though you can tweak it in the SteelSeries GG software. The spatial sound for games is immersive and accurate enough to help you pinpoint footsteps or the whomp of an approaching helicopter. With USB, Bluetooth 4.2, optical in and out, and 3.5-mm aux, your connectivity bases are covered. You can also sync the Prism RGB lighting with the rest of your setup, have it react to music, or just pick a color. On the downside, the speakers are quite tall, and the subwoofer is bulky and sometimes overpowers the sound.

Majority DX10 Desktop Speakers for £13: They lack bass and general clarity, but these USB-powered speakers are the cheapest I’ve tried. These 10-watt, 2.5-inch, full-range speakers are angled up toward your ears and have a simple power and volume dial. There’s also a 3.5 mm headphone port. Only available in the UK, they could be enough if your budget is very tight.

Edifier G2000 Pro for $212: A spruced-up version of the G2000 above, the Pro is an upgrade to 64-watt power, 3-inch full-range drivers, and virtual 7.1 surround sound. Edifier also made these speakers translucent and added garish RGB lighting effects courtesy of LED strips in each speaker. They do sound a bit better, though still lacking in bass, and some folks will love the sci-fi light show, but there isn’t enough extra to justify the significant jump in price.

Creative Pebble X Plus for $123: If our budget pick isn’t quite doing it for you, Creative’s Pebble X Plus adds a cube-shaped subwoofer under your desk. The larger speakers, with RGB lighting, are also more powerful, and the sub provides punchy bass. They sound reasonably good for the money. Connectivity is also beefed up compared to the V3 above, with headphone and microphone ports and Bluetooth 5.3, but all of this invariably comes at a higher cost.

Onkyo Creator GX-10DB for $250: Capable of producing a warm and rich sound, Onkyo’s speakers are the perfect size for your desktop and come with angled stands (though they are plastic). The connectivity options are solid, with USB-C, optical, and stereo RCA inputs, and support for Bluetooth 5.3. These speakers get a little louder than our top pick, though you’ll need to pair a subwoofer if you’re into bass (there is a subwoofer-out port). Sadly, the volume knob on the back of the right speaker is tricky to reach, the slim remote control has a weird layout, and the source LED on the front is always on. But what I struggled with most was the automatic power-off (Onkyo says this “feature” is an eco-regulation in Europe) that turns off the speakers if they aren’t used for 15 minutes. If you have more space and crave more power, I also tested the Onkyo Creator Series GX-30ARC ($350), which goes far louder and adds a decent thump of bass.

Creative Sound Blaster GS5 for $95: While it doesn’t quite have the power of the OXS Thunder Lite above, this soundbar is cheaper and matches it on connectivity, even adding cool RGB lighting to the underside. It also has a remote and decent software for making EQ and lighting adjustments. The sound lacks clarity, and the bass is limited, but this is a solid, small soundbar for the money and works well as a desktop device.

Logitech Z407 for $110: A complete 2.1 system at this price is no mean feat. These speakers connect via USB, 3.5-mm aux, or Bluetooth, and there’s a wireless remote volume dial. Construction is cheap, and the sound lacks definition, but there’s a good thump of bass from the subwoofer, and mids and highs are reasonably crisp, provided you don’t turn the volume up too high. WIRED senior reviews editor Julian Chokkattu says he used a variation of the Logitech Z-series for nearly a decade and only recently donated them to someone else.

Razer Nommo V2 X for $150: The sound quality of Razer’s entry-level speakers is solid for music and good for movies and games (there's THX Spatial support), though lacking in bass. These no-frills speakers look great but lack a subwoofer, RGB lighting, and a remote. They offer USB and Bluetooth connectivity and can be customized in Razer’s Synapse software.

These are the computer speakers that had deal-breaking flaws for me.

OXS Thunder Duo X for $550: These powerful speakers get plenty loud and come with a wireless neck speaker for surround sound, but they are very large (way too big for my desk) and, frankly, kinda garish when they light up. The sound quality is decent and I liked the surround sound for gaming, but the neck speaker is not comfortable, especially for long gaming sessions (much will depend on your office chair). You can also get these speakers with a subwoofer.

OXS Thunder Lite for $150: This compact soundbar lacks the bells and whistles of its bigger sibling above, but is far more affordable. It can get plenty loud, supports virtual surround sound, and comes with a small remote. Unfortunately, separation was poor, so it was tough to tell where sounds were coming from in games, and it is severely lacking in bass for a soundbar with thunder in its name. Connectivity includes USB-C, 3.5-mm aux, optical, or HDMI, and it supports Bluetooth 5.0.

Edifier QR65 for $314: Delivering classy looks with supercool lighting effects and a seriously big, powerful sound, these speakers are excellent for music, movies, or games. They also come with two angled stands to point them at your ears. They have USB, RCA, and Bluetooth 5.3 connectivity and USB ports for charging your gadgets. Controls are decent, with a physical button on the right speaker for power and cycling through modes. The problem is that they are huge and won’t fit on most desktops, including mine.

Creative Stage V2 for $150: This affordable soundbar offers excellent connectivity with HDMI ARC, optical, USB, 3.5-mm aux, and Bluetooth 5.0. But it’s not especially powerful, can sound muddy and flat, and has a short cable (no good for sit-stand desks). The subwoofer lends some decent bass, there’s a remote control, and I like the Clear Dialog option to sharpen voices, but you can do better.

House of Marley Get Together Duo for $170: Sporting an attractive and eco-friendly blend of bamboo and fabric, the Get Together Duo from House of Marley is affordable. They connect via Bluetooth 5.0, RCA, or 3.5-mm aux. There’s no subwoofer, the midrange is dominant, and they are lacking something at the high end. The battery-powered right speaker can also double as a portable speaker, and you can use these as bookshelf speakers, but as computer speakers, they are just OK.

SteelSeries Arena 3 for $150: Sporting a nice pear-shaped design with tiltable speakers and subtle branding, the entry-level Arena 3 from SteelSeries can get loud. But they lack bass, lose detail in the highs, and sound a bit fuzzy for music. Even for SteelSeries fans, there isn’t much reason to choose these over some of our picks above. They don’t have lighting, USB, or any other extras.

Logitech Z906 5.1 Surround Sound Speaker System for $450: This 5.1 system is THX-certified and comes with a huge subwoofer, five speakers, and a central control unit. The design feels dated, maybe even a bit ugly, and you need to run cables around your room. The surround sound effect is solid, and you can even convert stereo with the 3D mode, but overall, it’s a bass-heavy system.

Budget is a deciding factor for most folks, but even cheap desktop speakers offer far better sound than your monitor. Headphones are a great alternative, but not everyone wants to wear headphones all the time. You can spend as much as you like on audio gear, but I have focused on reasonably affordable desktop systems here, starting from as low as $35 and not exceeding $700.

What Should I Look for in Computer Speakers?

It depends. There’s plenty to weigh when shopping for a set of computer speakers, so it’s vital to start by deciding what’s most important to you. For example, I work and play on the same desktop PC, so I need speakers that perform well for video calls, long gaming sessions, listening to music, and watching movies. I also have a standing desk, and my monitor setup doesn’t leave much room, so I prefer compact all-rounders with long cables.

Sound quality: The top consideration for most folks, you want the best sound quality you can afford. A good set of speakers will offer a balance of clear vocals, rich treble, and rumbling bass. If you crave bass you feel in the pit of your stomach, a subwoofer is essential, though it might not be a good idea for folks who have downstairs neighbors. For accurate positional sound, you might want to look at a surround sound system with multiple speakers.

Design: Consider the finish. Your speakers will be on show, so you’ll want to pick something that fits your decor.

Brand: Gamers with devices from an existing brand might lean toward the same brand of speakers because they can be configured in the same software. This is particularly important with speakers that have built-in lights, so you can sync up your entire setup.

Extras: Some people will consider these superfluous, but if you want a remote control for kicking back or RGB lighting to bring a splash of color to your desk, these are extra perks on higher-end speakers. Snag speakers with a decent range of connectivity, and you can always repurpose them later. Most speakers come with all the cables you need, but it’s worth checking before you buy. I have listed what you will find in the box with all the computer speakers I recommend.

Where Should I Position My Desktop Speakers?

You ideally want the speakers to be angled slightly up (around 15 degrees) and pointed at your ears. Since you know the exact spot you’ll be in when listening, you can tweak the position of your speakers for the best results. Don’t just chuck them on the desk and leave it at that. Try moving and angling them until you find that sweet spot.

Speaker stands can maximize sound quality by helping to reduce vibrations from your desktop that can muddy the sound. Angled speaker stands are also a good way to direct the sound toward your ears. Some manufacturers, such as Edifier and Onkyo, include stands; IK Multimedia and Razer include adjustable bases or fold-out feet; Audioengine sells stands separately. You will also find a wide choice of third-party stands online.

If space is limited, a compact set of speakers will work best. The trade-off is power and volume, as small speakers generally don’t produce as big or high-quality a sound as large speakers. If you opt for a subwoofer, you will want a suitable space under your desk. For surround sound systems, you must run cables and find suitable spots for speakers behind you. If you have a wide monitor on a mount, a compact soundbar beneath it could be the best fit. Check the dimensions carefully and measure the space on your desk before you buy.

What’s the Best Way to Connect My Speakers to My Computer?

Speakers can come with a multitude of ports and connectivity options. USB connections usually sound best because they output the digital signal for the digital-to-analog converter (DAC) in the speakers, which is likely to be better unless you have a good sound card. But the best way to be sure is to try both and see which sounds better. If you want to be able to connect a phone or laptop wirelessly, then Bluetooth is paramount. Most speakers have a 3.5-mm aux input, and some have an output for headphones. Just make sure your preferred speakers support the connectivity you want. You should also make sure that you have the necessary free ports on your PC or laptop, though you can always add more with a USB hub.

Every set of speakers in this guide was tested for at least a week, sometimes longer. I don’t use headphones, so they were all used for video calls throughout my work day, listening to music and podcasts, and for movies and games in the evening. While I played several games, watched many movies or shows, and listened to lots of music and podcasts, I ran through a specific list of test content with every speaker system to make it easier to compare them.

My test content included the game Halo Infinite, the movie Dune, and a music playlist including “Hip-Hop” (Dead Prez), “The National Anthem” (Radiohead), “All Along the Watchtower” (Jimi Hendrix), “Hey” (Pixies), “Sabotage” (Beastie Boys), “A Day in the Life” (the Beatles), “Nothing Compares 2 U” (Sinéad O'Connor), and “Only God Knows” (Young Fathers).

#341. The Download: a humanoid cleans house and Samsung builds for the AI boom

Plus: Almost $2.5 trillion has been wiped off tech stocks.

This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.

When I saw an X post about a new humanoid-robot cleaning service in San Francisco, I immediately signed up for the waitlist. I wanted my apartment to feel like The Jetsons, even if just for an hour.

The device that arrived at my building belongs to Tau Robotics, a local startup. Its long-term goal is to make autonomous cleaning robots a reality, but the technology isn’t quite there yet. For now, humans pilot the robots remotely, watching them work through onboard cameras.

#340. Ilse Aigner tipped by party allies as next German president

German media reports suggest that Bavarian politician Ilse Aigner's chances of becoming the next president are on the up. Long favored by her Bavarian CSU, now it seems Christian Democrats nationwide plan to back her.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (the CDU) and their Bavarian sister party, the CSU, want to nominate a joint candidate to be the next president of Germany when the special "Bundesversammlung" committee that elects one votes at the end of January.

It's long been clear that the CSU favor the current speaker of Bavaria's parliament, Ilse Aigner, for the role.

But on Friday, multiple German news outlets like Spiegel, the Süddeutsche Zeitung and the DPA news agency cited sources in the CDU as saying that party's leadership had also decided on putting Aigner forward.

DPA reported that Merz would officially recommend Aigner as a candidate at a meeting of the CDU's leadership that will convene in Berlin on Sunday and Monday.

On the record, however, party officials would neither confirm nor deny the reports, pointing only to the upcoming meetings on Monday.

If chosen, Aigner would be the 13th person and the first woman to take up the role as post-war Germany's head of state, which is a more ceremonial one with primarily symbolic power, while the bulk of the political and legislative power resides with the chancellor.

She would also be the first CSU politician to hold the office.

Aigner, 61, is currently the speaker of the state parliament in Bavaria.

The youngest of four sisters and the daughter of an electrician, she worked in the family business in her early adult life before going into politics. She's a Roman Catholic, single and has no children.

Aigner began her parliamentary career in the Bavarian legislature in 1994, then moved to the Bundestag federal parliament in 1998, before returning to the Bavarian chamber in 2013.

She spent five years as federal agriculture minister under then-Chancellor Angela Merkel.

She would also be the first CSU politician to hold the office.

Current President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, a heavy hitter for years for the Social Democrats before becoming head of state, is nearing the end of his second five-year term in the role, having assumed the office in March 2017.

The CDU/CSU's junior coalition partners, the Social Democrats (SPD), have also made it clear they would back a presidential bid from Aigner.

"If the CDU steering committee does indeed officially assert itself on Monday and put forward Ilse Aigner, then on behalf of the SPD I can only say that we would welcome this and support it," SPD chairman Lars Klingbeil said at an event in Berlin.

A large committee known as the Bundesversammlung chooses the German president. It will vote on January 30, 2027.

It's made up of all 630 Bundestag parliament members, and another 630 people assigned to represent the various German states — weighted according to each state's share of the national population.

Most of these are regional lawmakers, but municipal politicians and people from other walks of public life are also sometimes given a vote.

The CDU/CSU and SPD combined have a majority of roughly 50 seats in the special committee.

Beyond this, Merz is expected to try to rope in support for Aigner from the Greens, a party that has long championed more female representation at the top of politics and that would not seem to have a realistic chance of propelling a candidate of its own into the role.

This suggests that if Aigner's nomination were to materialize and solidify, she should have fairly good chances of succeeding Steinmeier.

#337. It's a weird time to buy a laptop, but the new MacBook Pro doesn't skimp on quality

It has the best laptop screen we’ve used, but there may be reasons to wait.

Apple’s new MacBook Pro is expensive as hell.

Let’s get that out there right away, because for a lot of people, it will be the only thing that matters. As with so many things in life, though, you get what you pay for. There’s no questioning the quality of the laptop’s display or most of its other hardware components.

But should you buy it? Well, that’s a complicated question in 2026.

We’re in a time of great uncertainty when it comes to buying a computer. Prices are at levels we’ve not seen in recent history, and they may well keep climbing. Meanwhile, users paying close attention to the early developments in both local and agentic artificial intelligence are asking an important question: “What will computing even look like in a few years, and what does that mean for the computer I should buy today?”

Apple’s new MacBook Pro sits at the intersection of all of this uncertainty. In multiple ways, it’s also straddling different worlds.

It arrives amid a changing of the guard in Apple’s leadership, potentially raising questions about the future direction of Apple’s ecosystem. It’s a mass-market consumer product, but configuring it with enough RAM and storage to make it feel future-proof pushes its price into territory mostly only well-funded businesses can afford. It’s firmly rooted in the computing paradigms of the past 20 years, but it shows early signs of flirtation with new AI workflows. It’s a conventional Apple laptop in most ways, but it also has a touchscreen—something that would never have happened in a prior Apple era.

It’s an outstanding, high-quality product, but whether it’s something you should buy depends on you—what you’re doing right now, what you’ll be doing in the future, and what you value.

For most of the specs we look at, Apple isn’t claiming any difference here. The new MacBook Pro promises 24 hours of battery life (though you’d have to use it in a conservative way to achieve that), it has the same ports (three Thunderbolt, one HDMI, one SDXC, and MagSafe), and it has the N1 chip for Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 connectivity.

And like its immediate predecessor, it offers the M5 Pro and M5 Max chips as options. Running synthetic benchmarks, we found no meaningful difference at all compared to when we ran the same tests on the previous model, so we won’t spend time discussing their performance today. We’ve covered both thoroughly in prior reviews, and you can read up there if you’d like.

The chips are more than fast enough for normal workflows for the foreseeable future, including most 3D work. AI inference is the main area where they may be less future-proof. To be clear, they’re strong enough for now, but the field is evolving rapidly, and there’s reason to expect significant improvements in future chips on this front.

According to Bloomberg, Apple is skipping Pro and Max versions of the M6 chip that was introduced earlier this year to focus its attention on a significant rework for the M7 due in 2027. “The M7 line is designed primarily around major advancements to on-device AI processing,” Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman wrote. The line would emphasize memory bandwidth, which matters for fast, efficient AI inference.

Even without Bloomberg’s report, I’d expect Apple to prioritize those areas in its next high-end chip refresh. That’s partly because there’s another tea leaf to read here: Apple made just such an update with the A20 Pro, which debuted in its latest iPhones several weeks ago. That update brought a substantially improved Neural Engine and a significant increase in memory bandwidth. We also found that the A20 Pro delivered improved 3D graphics performance in some cases.

Similar improvements could come to Macs, meaning it might be worth waiting another year if you’re focused on AI workflows or even 3D applications—especially given the high cost of these machines. That’s part of what makes this such an uncertain time to buy a laptop. We’re in a moment when these companies are revisiting the architecture of these chips because of these new workflows, and we don’t know what the end result is yet.

Here’s one thing that’s not at all uncertain: The display on the MacBook Pro is the best I have ever used in a laptop. If the display is your primary concern, this is a big moment.

Apple calls it a “tandem OLED display,” meaning a panel with two emissive layers. This approach helps achieve a higher peak brightness, but perhaps more importantly, it can reduce the risk of burn-in. Most of the time, the display won’t need both layers running at full power. Instead, they can share the load and run at a reduced current, helping extend the panel’s lifespan.

The new display can achieve up to 2,000 nits of peak brightness on HDR highlights, but it’s rated for 1,000 nits of sustained brightness. In general, I like the way Apple handles HDR for this at the OS level, too.

The brightness matters for HDR content, sure, but what really makes OLED stand out is per-pixel illumination—meaning each pixel can turn on or off independently. That allows for absolute black levels and very strong contrast. The MiniLED display in the previous MacBook Pro offered good contrast for an LCD display, but OLED has a fundamental advantage here, and it shows.

As you’d expect, the screen offers native support for both P3 and Adobe RGB color gamuts. It also has a variable refresh rate from 10 to 120 Hz, just like many of Apple’s other products. As before, the MacBook Pro comes in roughly 14-inch (3,024×1,986 pixels) and 16-inch (3,472×2,226 pixels) variants. There’s also a nano-texture glass option to fight glare, though that will set you back another $150.

It’s one of the most impressive displays I’ve used in any device, and it’s certainly the best I’ve ever used on a laptop. The colors are vibrant, the contrast is outstanding, the blacks are inky, and it can get very bright when it needs to—not just with highlights but full-screen brightness as well. And on the whole, it’s extremely precise. Uniformity appears basically flawless. It’s what you’d expect from an ultra-high-end TV or reference monitor, not a laptop or computer screen, and it’s genuinely striking.

We’ll see about longevity, but OLED has come a long way in recent years, and my first impressions are that Apple has made all the right choices here.

I find myself trying to find something negative to say about the MacBook Pro’s screen to avoid sounding too effusive, but I can’t think of anything substantive. The best I can do is complain that Apple’s proprietary “PROLED XDR” label is silly and eye-roll-inducing.

Branding aside, the screen is the main reason to pay extra for this model.

With its lid closed, the new MacBook Pro looks identical to its predecessor. The dimensions are largely the same. It’s slightly thinner, but you’d have to check the spec sheet or handle them side by side to notice.

Pick it up, though, and you’ll find that it’s noticeably lighter than the last model, by about half a pound. It’s not in a totally different weight class, but you can notice the change, and it’s a nice improvement. The reduction is partly due to the display technology switch; it’s easier to make a light OLED screen than a light MiniLED one.

Open the MacBook Pro and turn it on, and you’ll see one of a few other notable differences, depending on whether you’re behind or in front of it. From behind, you’ll see the Apple logo on the lid now lights up, as it did on MacBooks of yore. It’s arguably a little tacky, but it’s also neat and nostalgic. I don’t hate it.

From the front, you might notice that the already barely there bezels are even more barely there, though that’s subtle. More likely, you’ll see that the top-of-screen camera notch has been replaced by a cutout just like the Dynamic Island Apple introduced on the iPhone.

When I reviewed the first iPhone with a Dynamic Island, I was largely positive about it. No, it’s not ideal to have a cutout on the screen, but Apple has handled it as intelligently as possible, and I would even go so far as to say it has turned what should be an albatross into an attractive feature.

Thanks to the OLED display, it’s possible to make any of the pixels around the camera cutout just as black as it is. Apple has designed live activities, the volume bar, and more to appear as if they are expanding out of and around, and contracting back into, this little dot. It remains ingenious.

When the Dynamic Island first arrived on the iPhone, it helped unify several previously disparate approaches to displaying notifications in iOS, making it especially useful. This time, it doesn’t solve as many problems, but it’s an improvement over the dead weight of the notch. It also helps that the MacBook Pro’s much larger screen means the cutout takes up a small share of the screen’s real estate.

The Dynamic Island works the same with full-screen apps as the notch did. By default, the top of the viewport ends just below the Dynamic Island, so it just looks like there’s a taller top bezel, and it doesn’t cut into the application interface. The menu bar, clock, and other system elements still occupy the space above the application (set against a totally black background) when you move the cursor up there.

I tested a few fullscreen games with it, like World of Warcraft and Cyberpunk 2077. Some behaved by default like the default fullscreen app behavior I just described, but others tried to occupy the whole thing, making the cutout visible. Vitally, every video app I tried avoided the cutout in fullscreen.

This isn’t something to upgrade for, of course. But on the whole, I think it’s an improvement over what we had before.

Apple has finally added a touchscreen to the MacBook Pro. I say “finally” because the possibility has floated around for about two decades. Steve Jobs was famously opposed to the idea; there’s even video of him explaining why he thought it would make for a poor user experience.

A couple of years ago, reliable reports emerged that Apple was moving forward with the idea regardless. When I first heard about it, I imagined what could be a really exciting implementation: a convertible laptop that would let you use it in a tablet-like mode, with Apple Pencil support for drawing and writing.

As a game developer, I imagined quickly sketching 2D game maps with an Apple Pencil, using a local AI model to convert them into 3D geometry, and then switching to a laptop configuration to start testing and coding. I also imagined using it like an iPad to more comfortably watch movies on a flight.

That’s not what we got, though. The laptop has the same form factor as the previous MacBook Pro model—no tablet mode or Pencil support. Instead, it just lets you reach up from the keyboard and trackpad to touch the screen. That feels like a missed opportunity.

Some creative apps have implemented touch features that might justify the touchscreen functionality if you use them a lot. For example, you can play the on-screen virtual piano keys on Logic Pro with multiple fingers, which could be nicer than clicking on them. I imagine many people already have workflows built around other approaches, though.

If you were specifically waiting for a touchscreen on your MacBook Pro, this seems like as good an implementation as you could hope for without turning the laptop into a convertible. Apple has put real care into it. For example, it has re-engineered the hinge so the screen is not particularly wobbly when you touch it. It’s fast, accurate, and responsive. It supports multi-touch gestures like pinch-to-zoom or swiping with three fingers to switch desktop spaces.

There’s one use case I find compelling as a developer. Testing iPhone and iPad apps in the Simulator has always been a minor hassle because of the difference in input methods. You either have to approximate only a subset of the interactions available to users with a trackpad and mouse or connect an iPhone or iPad to test them that way. A touchscreen could provide a more elegant way to test such apps in Xcode, Unity, or whatever else you might use.

Unfortunately, some of the UI elements in macOS are too small for my large fingers, so I have to tap very carefully. I also keep forgetting the touchscreen is even there for hours at a time and go back to my normal habits, partly because there’s nothing you can do at the OS level that you can’t do just as easily with trackpad gestures. And as Jobs predicted all those years ago, my arm got tired while I was using it.

For me, it feels faster, easier, more comfortable, and more natural to use the keyboard and trackpad 100 percent of the time, but I admittedly have decades of muscle memory and habits built around them. There’s apparently a generation coming up with the same kind of familiarity with touch interfaces, so this feature may appeal to them. Plus, touchscreen laptops have been a thing on Windows forever, and some people seem to want to buy them, though I never quite got why without an added tablet configuration.

It’s unlikely to account for a big portion of the device’s cost compared with the rest of the OLED panel, memory, storage, and so on. So, my own bafflement aside, I’m not unhappy it’s here. I imagine it will serve those who want it well enough.

As noted earlier, whether this laptop is worthy of a recommendation depends on you and how you use your machine. That’s always been the case, but it seems more so here.

If you’re a creative professional or a display enthusiast who wants the best laptop screen you’ve likely ever seen, you won’t be disappointed if you shell out for it. And hey, maybe you can show me your workflow and prove me wrong about the touchscreen!

If you’re just looking for a great laptop with strong performance for everyday use, consider the non-OLED, non-touchscreen model that’s still in Apple’s lineup—or even a MacBook Air, which compromises relatively little for most users. And there is, of course, the entire world of Windows and Linux laptops.

If you’re a developer—especially one working at the frontier of AI workflows—well, that’s where things get tricky. Will waiting be worthwhile? So much about how those workflows will evolve and what they’ll demand from your hardware is still so up in the air that I can’t make a confident recommendation. (For what it’s worth, I fit best in this category, and I’m still holding onto my M1 Max machine, though my resolve is wavering.)

All that said, in most ways, this is still the same MacBook Pro we’ve reviewed again and again for the past few years. Touch adds a feature aimed at a particular niche, or perhaps it’s there to roll out the welcome mat for a newer generation. The display is a more substantial update and makes a compelling case for upgrading, especially if you’re coming from an older, pre-MiniLED laptop.

But this is an expensive machine. The configuration I reviewed here (16-inch, M5 Max, 128 GB of RAM, 2 TB SSD) retails for a whopping $7,399, though you could at least shave $1,600 off that by going to a more typical-for-most-people 64 GB. (The cheapest configuration starts at $2,899.)

For the vast majority of buyers, the pre-OLED version that’s still in Apple’s lineup or another MacBook altogether will offer more bang for your buck. If you’re the kind of person who wants OLED or a touchscreen, though, you probably know that already. Based on my time with the new MacBook Pro, both features deliver on their promises, even if the latter isn’t as ambitious as some of us had hoped.

#336. Moon phase today: What the Moon will look like on November 8, 2026

There's barely any of the Moon visible tonight as it approaches the New Moon. With less than a sliver illuminated, there is nothing for us to see in the way of lunar features.

As of Sunday, Nov. 8, the NASA's Daily Moon Guide tracker tells us the Moon is in the Waning Crescent phase, with 1% of its surface visible.

Visibility it too low tonight, so you won't be able to see any lunar features.

The next Full Moon will take place on November 24.

It takes the Moon around 29.5 days to pass through a complete lunar cycle. As it travels around Earth, the angle at which sunlight reaches its surface changes what we can see from here, producing the different phases, from the New Moon through to the Full Moon and back again. The cycle then starts over, as explained by NASA.

New Moon - The Moon is between Earth and the sun, so the side we see is dark (in other words, it's invisible to the eye).

Waxing Crescent - A small sliver of light appears on the right side (Northern Hemisphere).

First Quarter - Half of the Moon is lit on the right side. It looks like a half-Moon.

Waxing Gibbous - More than half is lit up, but it's not quite full yet.

Full Moon - The whole face of the Moon is illuminated and fully visible.

Waning Gibbous - The Moon starts losing light on the right side. (Northern Hemisphere)

Third Quarter (or Last Quarter) - Another half-Moon, but now the left side is lit.

Waning Crescent - A thin sliver of light remains on the left side before going dark again.

#335. How much Netflix cost in 2007 vs. 2026

The company is notorious for frequent price hikes.

Movie fans of a certain age may vividly remember the sad, somewhat rapid decline of the old video store. Whether your store of choice was the nearest Blockbuster or an independent shop, you probably smile at the nostalgia of heading to the video store on a Friday or Saturday night, anxiously hoping that a copy of the hottest new release was in stock. Or, better yet, just returned by another renter so you could swoop in and snag the last one.

Then streaming came along, and video stores around the world began fading into irrelevance, with locations closing as streaming services continued to grow in popularity. In 2006, Blockbuster — the undisputed king of video rental stores — made a last-ditch effort to stay current by offering Total Access, which allowed customers to exchange their mail-ordered DVD rentals in physical stores.

If you've only ever known Netflix as a streaming service on your smart TV, tablet or phone, you might find it interesting that, in 2007, Netflix could only be streamed on a Windows PC with Internet Explorer. And the video quality wasn't great. After all, high-definition (720p and 1080i) was just starting to take off as a mainstream viewing format in 2007. Netflix's streaming library of roughly 1,000 titles was pretty lean, as well. Its first original series was still five years away, and the first original Netflix movie didn't debut until 2015. But none of this stopped its prices from increasing — a true Netflix staple.

Over the next decade, Netflix added some new plans like Premium, Standard, Basic, Standard-definition-only, Basic with ads, Ad-Free and other iterations. And with those plans typically came annual price hikes, usually ranging from $1 to $3 more per month depending on the plan.

Today, Netflix offers three plans. Standard with ads costs $8.99 per month and includes ad-supported access to most (but not all) shows and movies in the Netflix catalog, with the ability to stream and download in 1080p HD on two supported devices at a time.
